Reduced-form VAR: theory, inference and use

Source: vignettes/var-theory.Rmd
var-theory.Rmd

This vignette defines the objects that varm computes for a reduced-form vector autoregression, states the formulas that the C++ engine implements, and says how to read the output economically. All examples use yraw, the quarterly US data of Koop and Korobilis: inflation, the unemployment rate and the short-term interest rate, 215 observations (1953Q1 to 2006Q3). Section numbers below follow the order in which a typical empirical project proceeds: specify, estimate, test, diagnose, identify, bootstrap, forecast.

The package computes estimates, impulse responses and forecasts; results come back as tibbles via tidy(), glance() and augment() and plot with autoplot() (ggplot2). The Wald/Granger tests and the residual diagnostics of Sections 4 and 5 are not package functions: wald_block(), portmanteau(), arch_lm(), jb_test() and the ACF helper are defined inside this vignette, built on coef(), fit$XtXinv, fit$Sigma and augment(), so do not look for them in the package. They are short enough to copy into your own scripts.

long <- do.call(rbind, lapply(vn, function(v) {
  data.frame(date = y$date, variable = v, value = y[[v]])
}))
ggplot(long, aes(date, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  facet_wrap(vars(variable), scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_varm()

1. The model

A VAR(pp) for the K×1K\times 1 vector yty_t is yt=c+∑l=1pAlyt−l+Γwt+ut,ut∼(0,Σ),E[utus′]=0(t≠s), y_t = c + \sum_{l=1}^{p} A_l\, y_{t-l} + \Gamma w_t + u_t,\qquad u_t \sim (0,\Sigma),\quad E[u_t u_s']=0\ (t\neq s), where wtw_t collects optional trend or exogenous regressors (trend = TRUE, exog =). Stacking regressors xt=(yt−1′,…,yt−p′,1,wt′)′x_t=(y_{t-1}',\dots,y_{t-p}',1,w_t')' gives Y=XB+UY = XB + U with BB the m×Km\times K coefficient matrix (m=Kp+dm=Kp+d), exactly the layout of fit$B (lags first, then deterministics; columns are equations).

Companion form. Define 𝐲t=(yt′,…,yt−p+1′)′\mathbf{y}_t=(y_t',\dots,y_{t-p+1}')'. Then 𝐲t=𝐜+𝐀𝐲t−1+𝐮t,𝐀=(A1A2⋯ApIK0⋯0⋱⋮0IK0). \mathbf{y}_t = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{A}\,\mathbf{y}_{t-1} + \mathbf{u}_t,\qquad \mathbf{A}=\begin{pmatrix}A_1&A_2&\cdots&A_p\\ I_K&0&\cdots&0\\ &\ddots&&\vdots\\ 0&&I_K&0\end{pmatrix}. The process is covariance stationary iff all eigenvalues of 𝐀\mathbf{A} lie inside the unit circle. stability() returns their moduli.

fit <- varm(y, p = 2)          # the Date column is dropped from the estimation, kept for plots
fit
#> <varm> VAR(2) with 3 variables, 213 effective observations
#> logLik = -338.416; max |eigenvalue| = 0.946
#> 
#>             infl   unemp    rate
#> infl.l1   1.5378 -0.0095  0.5457
#> unemp.l1 -0.2809  1.3297 -0.6475
#> rate.l1  -0.0571 -0.0210  0.7766
#> infl.l2  -0.5418  0.0341 -0.4395
#> unemp.l2  0.2336 -0.4290  0.6730
#> rate.l2   0.0580  0.0457  0.1232
#> const     0.2872  0.3654  0.0052
A <- lag_matrices(fit)           # array [K, K, p]: A[, , l] is the coefficient matrix on lag l
round(A[, , 1], 3)
#>         infl  unemp   rate
#> infl   1.538 -0.281 -0.057
#> unemp -0.010  1.330 -0.021
#> rate   0.546 -0.647  0.777
round(drop(stability(fit)), 3)   # moduli of the companion eigenvalues
#> [1] 0.946 0.946 0.746 0.746 0.432 0.139
glance(fit)                      # one-row summary: nobs, logLik, AIC, BIC, HQ, max_root
#> # A tibble: 1 × 8
#>       K     p  nobs logLik   AIC   BIC    HQ max_root
#>   <int> <int> <int>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>
#> 1     3     2   213  -338.  731.  822.  768.    0.946

varm(y, p = 2, vars = c(infl, rate)) fits a subset of the columns (tidyselect).

Moving-average representation. If the VAR is stable, yt=μ+∑h=0∞Φhut−h,Φ0=I,Φh=∑l=1min⁡(h,p)Φh−lAl. y_t = \mu + \sum_{h=0}^{\infty}\Phi_h u_{t-h},\quad \Phi_0=I,\quad \Phi_h=\sum_{l=1}^{\min(h,p)}\Phi_{h-l}A_l . The Φh\Phi_h are the reduced-form impulse responses to the innovations utu_t. They are not yet responses to economically meaningful shocks, because the elements of utu_t are contemporaneously correlated (see vignette("identification")).

Economic intuition / how to use it

The largest eigenvalue modulus is a persistence summary: the response of any variable to any shock decays roughly like |λmax|h|\lambda_{\max}|^h. For macro data in levels the value is typically 0.9 or above, which is why long-horizon VAR results are fragile (an eigenvalue of 0.98 versus 1.00 is not distinguishable in 200 quarterly observations, but the implied long-run behaviour differs completely). If the modulus exceeds one the model is explosive and forecasts and IRFs should not be trusted; for Bayesian fits stability(fit) returns a matrix of moduli across draws, so you can report the share of explosive draws.

2. Estimation and the covariance of the estimates

Equation-by-equation OLS, B̂=(X′X)−1X′Y\hat B=(X'X)^{-1}X'Y, equals Gaussian maximum likelihood for BB because all equations share the same regressors. The residual covariance is estimated with two normalisations, Σ̂ML=Û′ÛTe,Σ̂=Û′ÛTe−m, \hat\Sigma_{ML}=\frac{\hat U'\hat U}{T_e},\qquad \hat\Sigma=\frac{\hat U'\hat U}{T_e-m}, with Te=T−pT_e=T-p effective observations. fit$Sigma is the degrees-of-freedom corrected Σ̂\hat\Sigma; fit$Sigma_ml is the ML version. The Gaussian log-likelihood at the optimum is ℓ=−TeK2log⁡(2π)−Te2log⁡|Σ̂ML|−TeK2. \ell=-\tfrac{T_e K}{2}\log(2\pi)-\tfrac{T_e}{2}\log|\hat\Sigma_{ML}|-\tfrac{T_e K}{2}. For a stable VAR, Tevec(B̂−B)→dN(0,Σ⊗Q−1)\sqrt{T_e}\,\mathrm{vec}(\hat B-B)\overset{d}{\to}N\!\big(0,\Sigma\otimes Q^{-1}\big) with Q=plimX′X/TeQ=\mathrm{plim}\,X'X/T_e, so the standard errors reported by summary() are sê(B̂ik)=[(X′X)−1]iiΣ̂kk. \widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat B_{ik})=\sqrt{\big[(X'X)^{-1}\big]_{ii}\,\hat\Sigma_{kk}} . (fit$XtXinv stores (X′X)−1(X'X)^{-1}.) This is the same formula used by lm() in each equation, which we can verify:

d <- as.data.frame(embed(as.matrix(yraw), 3))
names(d) <- c(paste0(vn, ".l0"), paste0(vn, ".l1"), paste0(vn, ".l2"))
m1 <- lm(rate.l0 ~ infl.l1 + unemp.l1 + rate.l1 + infl.l2 + unemp.l2 + rate.l2, d)
cbind(lm = coef(m1)[-1], varm = coef(fit)[1:6, "rate"])[1:3, ]
#>                  lm       varm
#> infl.l1   0.5456700  0.5456700
#> unemp.l1 -0.6474938 -0.6474938
#> rate.l1   0.7766035  0.7766035
max(abs(summary(m1)$coefficients[-1, 2] - summary(fit)$se[1:6, "rate"]))
#> [1] 2.206568e-14

tidy() returns the same numbers in long form, one row per equation and regressor (response, term, estimate, std.error, statistic, p.value, and conf.low/conf.high with conf.int = TRUE):

s <- summary(fit)
co <- tidy(fit, conf.int = TRUE)
co[co$response == "rate", ]
#> # A tibble: 7 × 8
#>   response term     estimate std.error statistic  p.value conf.low conf.high
#>   <chr>    <chr>       <dbl>     <dbl>     <dbl>    <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1 rate     infl.l1   0.546      0.149     3.66   3.16e- 4   0.252      0.839
#> 2 rate     unemp.l1 -0.647      0.155    -4.17   4.47e- 5  -0.954     -0.341
#> 3 rate     rate.l1   0.777      0.0738   10.5    5.19e-21   0.631      0.922
#> 4 rate     infl.l2  -0.440      0.153    -2.87   4.52e- 3  -0.741     -0.138
#> 5 rate     unemp.l2  0.673      0.148     4.55   9.03e- 6   0.382      0.964
#> 6 rate     rate.l2   0.123      0.0726    1.70   9.10e- 2  -0.0198     0.266
#> 7 rate     const     0.00517    0.238     0.0217 9.83e- 1  -0.465      0.475
round(s$r.squared, 3)
#>  infl unemp  rate 
#> 0.983 0.949 0.928

Economic intuition / how to use it

The interest-rate equation is a reaction function in reduced form: the coefficient on lagged inflation is the central bank’s response (together with everything else correlated with it) and the very large own-lag coefficient is interest-rate smoothing. Individual VAR coefficients are rarely interpreted one by one; they are highly collinear and their signs depend on the lag order. Use them for (i) Granger-causality style tests of a block of coefficients, (ii) diagnosing stability, and (iii) as the input to the dynamic objects below. The residual correlation matrix printed by summary() is the first diagnostic of identification: large correlations mean the Cholesky ordering will matter.

round(cor(resid(fit)), 2)
#>        infl unemp  rate
#> infl   1.00 -0.04  0.11
#> unemp -0.04  1.00 -0.35
#> rate   0.11 -0.35  1.00

The residuals are also available next to the data through augment(), which pads the first pp rows with NA; the diagnostics of Section 5 start from it.

Degrees-of-freedom conventions, in one place

quantity divisor where
Σ̂\hat\Sigma (fit$Sigma, vcov(fit)) Te−mT_e-m standard errors, t-tests, bootstrap and MC draws of Σ\Sigma, IRF (default Cholesky)
Σ̂ML\hat\Sigma_{ML} (fit$Sigma_ml) TeT_e log-likelihood, information criteria
t-test reference distribution tTe−mt_{T_e-m} summary(fit)$pvalue
nobs(fit) Te=T−pT_e=T-p glance(fit)$nobs

where m=Kp+dm=Kp+d is the number of regressors per equation. The logLik() degrees of freedom are mK+K(K+1)/2mK+K(K+1)/2 (here 27 for p=2p=2).

c(Te = nobs(fit), m = fit$npar)
#>  Te   m 
#> 213   7
all.equal(fit$Sigma, fit$Sigma_ml * nobs(fit) / (nobs(fit) - fit$npar), check.attributes = FALSE)
#> [1] TRUE
logLik(fit)
#> 'log Lik.' -338.4159 (df=27)

t-tests

Under Gaussian errors B̂ik/sê(B̂ik)∼tTe−m\hat B_{ik}/\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\hat B_{ik})\sim t_{T_e-m} exactly when the regressors are strictly exogenous, and asymptotically N(0,1)N(0,1) in a stable VAR. summary(fit)$pvalue uses 2Pr⁡(tTe−m>|t|)2\Pr(t_{T_e-m}>|t|). These tests apply to one coefficient at a time; to test whether a whole variable matters use the Wald tests of the next section, because lags of the same variable are strongly collinear and individually insignificant even when jointly very significant.

3. Choosing the lag order

On a common sample of Te=T−pmaxT_e=T-p_{\max} observations, let Σ̃(p)=Ûp′Ûp/Te\tilde\Sigma(p)=\hat U_p'\hat U_p/T_e and np=pK2+Kdn_p=pK^2+Kd the number of mean parameters. var_select() reports AIC(p)=log⁡|Σ̃(p)|+2Tenp,HQ(p)=log⁡|Σ̃(p)|+2log⁡log⁡TeTenp,SC(p)=log⁡|Σ̃(p)|+log⁡TeTenp,log⁡FPE(p)=Klog⁡Te+Kp+dTe−Kp−d+log⁡|Σ̃(p)|.\begin{align} \mathrm{AIC}(p)&=\log|\tilde\Sigma(p)|+\frac{2}{T_e}n_p,\\ \mathrm{HQ}(p)&=\log|\tilde\Sigma(p)|+\frac{2\log\log T_e}{T_e}n_p,\\ \mathrm{SC}(p)&=\log|\tilde\Sigma(p)|+\frac{\log T_e}{T_e}n_p,\\ \log\mathrm{FPE}(p)&=K\log\frac{T_e+Kp+d}{T_e-Kp-d}+\log|\tilde\Sigma(p)|. \end{align} These are Lütkepohl’s (2005) formulas (the FPE is returned on the log scale, which has the same argmin) and the selected lags agree with vars::VARselect(). Because the sample is common, a criterion value is comparable across pp but not across different pmax.

sel <- var_select(y, pmax = 8)
sel$selection
#> AIC  HQ  SC FPE 
#>   6   2   2   6
round(sel$criteria, 3)
#>      AIC     HQ     SC    FPE
#> 1 -4.694 -4.616 -4.501 -4.694
#> 2 -5.217 -5.081 -4.879 -5.217
#> 3 -5.238 -5.043 -4.755 -5.238
#> 4 -5.239 -4.985 -4.611 -5.239
#> 5 -5.347 -5.035 -4.575 -5.346
#> 6 -5.372 -5.001 -4.455 -5.371
#> 7 -5.346 -4.916 -4.283 -5.343
#> 8 -5.308 -4.820 -4.101 -5.305
crit <- data.frame(
  p = rep(seq_len(nrow(sel$criteria)), ncol(sel$criteria)),
  criterion = rep(colnames(sel$criteria), each = nrow(sel$criteria)),
  value = as.vector(sel$criteria)
)
best <- data.frame(p = unname(sel$selection), criterion = names(sel$selection))
best$value <- mapply(function(p, cr) sel$criteria[p, cr], best$p, best$criterion)
ggplot(crit, aes(p, value)) +
  geom_line(colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  geom_point(colour = varm_palette(1)) +
  geom_point(data = best, colour = varm_palette(2)[2], size = 3, shape = 1, stroke = 1.2) +
  facet_wrap(vars(criterion), nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Lag order p", y = "Criterion (minimum circled)") +
  theme_varm()

Economic intuition / how to use it

AIC and FPE penalise parameters lightly and tend to overfit in small samples, whereas SC and HQ are consistent and pick short lags. A sensible workflow is to take the SC/HQ choice as a baseline, check residual autocorrelation (Section 5), and use a longer lag only if short lags leave serial correlation. More lags is not free: the number of parameters grows as pK2pK^2. With K=3K=3 and p=6p=6 there are 54 slope coefficients for about 209 observations. If you need long lags with many variables, use a Bayesian VAR (vignette("bayesian-var")), which shrinks the extra parameters.

4. Wald tests, Granger causality and block exogeneity

Definition. Because Var(vecB̂)=Σ⊗(X′X)−1\mathrm{Var}(\mathrm{vec}\,\hat B)=\Sigma\otimes(X'X)^{-1} (vec stacks the columns of B̂\hat B, i.e. equation by equation), any linear hypothesis H0:Rvec(B)=0H_0:R\,\mathrm{vec}(B)=0 is tested with W=vec(B̂)′R′[R(Σ̂⊗(X′X)−1)R′]−1Rvec(B̂)∼aχ2(r),F=W/r≈F(r,Te−m). W=\mathrm{vec}(\hat B)'R'\big[R(\hat\Sigma\otimes(X'X)^{-1})R'\big]^{-1}R\,\mathrm{vec}(\hat B)\ \overset{a}{\sim}\ \chi^2(r), \qquad F=W/r\ \approx\ F(r,\,T_e-m). Variable jjdoes not Granger-cause variable kk if the coefficients on all pp lags of jj in equation kk are zero (r=pr=p). A block-exogeneity test generalises this to a set of variables JJ not entering a set of equations GG (r=p|J||G|r=p|J||G|). Granger causality is about predictive content, not structural causation: a variable that anticipates the future (an interest rate that responds to expected inflation) will “cause” the variable it responds to. varm has no dedicated function for these tests. The helper wald_block() below is defined in this vignette; it is not exported by the package. It uses only fit$B, fit$XtXinv and fit$Sigma, and takes variable names as strings.

# H0: variables `from` do not enter equations `to` (all lags). Returns Wald/F statistics.
wald_block <- function(fit, from, to = setdiff(fit$varnames, from)) {
  K <- fit$K; p <- fit$p; m <- nrow(fit$B); vn <- fit$varnames
  idx <- c(outer(sort(match(from, vn)) , (seq_len(p) - 1) * K, "+"))   # rows of B for lags of `from`
  cols <- match(to, vn)
  sel <- unlist(lapply(cols, function(k) (k - 1) * m + idx))           # positions in vec(B)
  V <- kronecker(fit$Sigma, fit$XtXinv)[sel, sel, drop = FALSE]
  b <- c(fit$B)[sel]
  W <- drop(t(b) %*% solve(V, b)); r <- length(sel)
  c(Wald = W, df = r, p_chisq = pchisq(W, r, lower.tail = FALSE),
    F = W / r, p_F = pf(W / r, r, nobs(fit) - m, lower.tail = FALSE))
}
tab <- t(sapply(vn, function(v) wald_block(fit, from = v, to = setdiff(vn, v))))
round(tab, 4)                                  # row = causing variable; H0: does not help predict the others
#>          Wald df p_chisq       F    p_F
#> infl  33.8805  4  0.0000  8.4701 0.0000
#> unemp 40.1811  4  0.0000 10.0453 0.0000
#> rate   9.9457  4  0.0414  2.4864 0.0447
round(wald_block(fit, "rate", "infl"), 4)     # a single pair
#>    Wald      df p_chisq       F     p_F 
#>  4.0282  2.0000  0.1334  2.0141  0.1361
round(wald_block(fit, c("infl", "unemp"), "rate"), 4)  # the rate equation ignores both
#>    Wald      df p_chisq       F     p_F 
#> 36.4323  4.0000  0.0000  9.1081  0.0000
# cross-check one case against nested lm() fits (F test of the rate lags in the inflation equation)
d2 <- as.data.frame(embed(as.matrix(yraw), 3)); names(d2) <- paste0(rep(vn, 3), ".l", rep(0:2, each = 3))
full <- lm(infl.l0 ~ infl.l1 + unemp.l1 + rate.l1 + infl.l2 + unemp.l2 + rate.l2, d2)
rest <- update(full, . ~ . - rate.l1 - rate.l2)
c(lm_F = anova(rest, full)$F[2], wald_F = unname(wald_block(fit, "rate", "infl")["F"]))
#>     lm_F   wald_F 
#> 2.014086 2.014086

The two F statistics agree exactly in the single-equation case, which confirms that the Kronecker covariance is implemented as stated.

Economic intuition / how to use it

Use the table as a map of the system’s information flow before interpreting any IRF. If the policy rate Granger-causes neither inflation nor unemployment, any “policy shock” IRF will be weakly identified in the sense of being small relative to noise; if a variable is block-exogenous to the rest (a world commodity price vis-a-vis a small economy) it can be ordered first in a Cholesky scheme and, if you want, estimated as an exogenous block. Test results depend on pp and on the other variables in the system (omitted-variable causality), so report them for a lag order that passes the diagnostics below.

5. Residual diagnostics

A VAR is only as good as its residuals: inference (Section 4), bootstrap bands and the Cholesky decomposition all assume the innovations are serially uncorrelated and (for the iid bootstrap) homoskedastic. Three checks follow. As with the Wald test, they are helper functions defined in this vignette (portmanteau(), arch_lm(), jb_test(); none is exported by varm). All of them start from augment(fit): the .resid_* columns hold the residuals and are NA for the first pp rows, which the helper resid_matrix() drops.

Autocorrelation (multivariate portmanteau, adjusted). With Ĉj=Te−1∑tûtût−j′\hat C_j=T_e^{-1}\sum_{t}\hat u_t\hat u_{t-j}', Qh=Te2∑j=1h1Te−jtr(Ĉj′Ĉ0−1ĈjĈ0−1)∼aχ2(K2(h−p)). Q_h=T_e^2\sum_{j=1}^{h}\frac{1}{T_e-j}\,\mathrm{tr}\big(\hat C_j'\hat C_0^{-1}\hat C_j\hat C_0^{-1}\big)\ \overset{a}{\sim}\ \chi^2\big(K^2(h-p)\big). ARCH-LM. For each equation regress ût2\hat u_t^2 on qq of its own lags and a constant; TeR2∼aχ2(q)T_e R^2\overset{a}{\sim}\chi^2(q) under conditional homoskedasticity. Normality (Jarque-Bera). Orthogonalise with the Cholesky factor of Σ̂ML\hat\Sigma_{ML}, êt=P−1ût\hat e_t=P^{-1}\hat u_t, then JBk=Te(ŝk2/6+(κ̂k−3)2/24)∼χ2(2)\mathrm{JB}_k=T_e\big(\hat s_k^2/6+(\hat\kappa_k-3)^2/24\big)\sim\chi^2(2) for each component (ŝ,κ̂\hat s,\hat\kappa = skewness and kurtosis), and ∑kJBk∼χ2(2K)\sum_k\mathrm{JB}_k\sim\chi^2(2K).

resid_matrix <- function(fit) {
  a <- augment(fit)
  r <- a[startsWith(names(a), ".resid_")]
  r <- as.matrix(r[-seq_len(fit$p), ])
  colnames(r) <- sub(".resid_", "", colnames(r), fixed = TRUE)
  r
}
portmanteau <- function(fit, h = 12) {
  U <- resid_matrix(fit); Te <- nrow(U); C0i <- solve(crossprod(U) / Te)
  Q <- 0
  for (j in 1:h) { Cj <- crossprod(U[-(1:j), ], U[1:(Te - j), ]) / Te
                   Q <- Q + sum(diag(t(Cj) %*% C0i %*% Cj %*% C0i)) / (Te - j) }
  Q <- Te^2 * Q; df <- fit$K^2 * (h - fit$p)
  c(Q = Q, df = df, p = pchisq(Q, df, lower.tail = FALSE))
}
arch_lm <- function(fit, q = 4) {
  U <- resid_matrix(fit)
  sapply(colnames(U), function(v) {
    e2 <- U[, v]^2; Z <- embed(e2, q + 1)
    r2 <- summary(lm(Z[, 1] ~ Z[, -1]))$r.squared; st <- nrow(Z) * r2
    c(LM = st, p = pchisq(st, q, lower.tail = FALSE))
  })
}
jb_test <- function(fit) {
  U <- resid_matrix(fit); Te <- nrow(U)
  E <- U %*% t(solve(t(chol(fit$Sigma_ml))))          # e_t = P^{-1} u_t with P = chol lower
  s <- colMeans(E^3) / colMeans(E^2)^1.5; k <- colMeans(E^4) / colMeans(E^2)^2
  jb <- Te * (s^2 / 6 + (k - 3)^2 / 24)
  rbind(skew = s, kurt = k, JB = jb, p = pchisq(jb, 2, lower.tail = FALSE))
}
fit6 <- varm(y, p = 6)
round(rbind(`p=2` = portmanteau(fit, 12), `p=6` = portmanteau(fit6, 12)), 4)
#>            Q df      p
#> p=2 165.4792 90 0.0000
#> p=6  82.3773 54 0.0077
round(arch_lm(fit), 4)
#>       infl  unemp    rate
#> LM 29.7822 3.7408 47.5408
#> p   0.0000 0.4422  0.0000
round(jb_test(fit), 3)
#>        infl   unemp    rate
#> skew  0.271   1.176  -0.405
#> kurt  4.018   7.952  10.400
#> JB   11.808 266.691 491.820
#> p     0.003   0.000   0.000
# residual ACF from augment(): one panel per equation, approximate 95% bounds
U <- resid_matrix(fit)
acf_tbl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(colnames(U), function(v) {
  a <- acf(U[, v], lag.max = 16, plot = FALSE)
  data.frame(variable = v, lag = drop(a$lag)[-1], acf = drop(a$acf)[-1])
}))
ggplot(acf_tbl, aes(lag, acf)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(-1, 1) * 1.96 / sqrt(nrow(U)), linetype = 2, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = lag, yend = 0), colour = varm_palette(1), linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(vars(variable), nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Lag (quarters)", y = "Residual autocorrelation") +
  theme_varm()

Economic intuition / how to use it

A strongly significant portmanteau statistic at p=2p=2 means the lag order is too short (the persistent inflation and rate series need more dynamics): the standard errors, the Granger tests and the bands are then unreliable, and the remedy is to increase pp. The p=6p=6 row shows the statistic roughly halves, though the test still rejects at 1% with h=12h=12; in practice one would settle on a lag between the SC and AIC choices, or move to a Bayesian VAR, rather than chase a non-rejection. Rejection of ARCH-LM and normality is the norm for macro data (the volatility of the 1970s-80s was not that of the Great Moderation, and there are outliers around the 1970s oil shocks). Neither invalidates the point estimates, which only need E[ut|xt]=0E[u_t|x_t]=0, but they argue for the wild bootstrap (Section 8), which does not assume homoskedasticity, and against reading the Gaussian log-likelihood or the MC bands literally. Correct autocorrelation first; do not “fix” non-normality by adding lags.

6. Impulse responses, variance and historical decompositions

Write ut=Pεtu_t=P\varepsilon_t with PP′=ΣPP'=\Sigma and E[εtεt′]=IE[\varepsilon_t\varepsilon_t']=I. The structural moving-average coefficients are Θh=ΦhP\Theta_h=\Phi_h P and the response of variable ii at horizon hh to structural shock jj is IRFij(h)=ei′ΦhPej. \mathrm{IRF}_{ij}(h)=e_i'\,\Phi_h P\, e_j . irf() returns an object whose $estimate is an array [response, shock, horizon] (horizon 0 is impact). The default identification is a Cholesky factorisation; other choices of PP are the subject of vignette("identification"). With a Cholesky PP lower triangular, variable ii is allowed to react to shock jj on impact only if i≥ji\ge j in the ordering: the first variable is the “most exogenous” and the last responds to everything contemporaneously.

Forecast error variance decomposition. The hh-step forecast error is ∑s=0h−1Θsεt+h−s\sum_{s=0}^{h-1}\Theta_s\varepsilon_{t+h-s}, so the share of variable ii’s forecast error variance due to shock jj is FEVDij(h)=∑s=0h(ei′Θsej)2∑s=0h∑k=1K(ei′Θsek)2, \mathrm{FEVD}_{ij}(h)=\frac{\sum_{s=0}^{h}\big(e_i'\Theta_s e_j\big)^2}{\sum_{s=0}^{h}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\big(e_i'\Theta_s e_k\big)^2}, which sums to one over jj (fevd(); as implemented, index h=0h=0 is the impact decomposition and index hh cumulates horizons 0,…,h0,\dots,h).

Historical decomposition. Recursing the VAR from the initial conditions, yt=μ̂t⏟deterministic + initial conditions+∑j=1K∑s=0t−1Θsejε̂j,t−s⏟contribution of shock j,ε̂t=P−1ût, y_{t}= \underbrace{\hat\mu_t}_{\text{deterministic + initial conditions}}+ \sum_{j=1}^{K}\underbrace{\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}\Theta_s e_j\,\hat\varepsilon_{j,t-s}}_{\text{contribution of shock } j}, \qquad \hat\varepsilon_t=P^{-1}\hat u_t , so that the observed path is exactly the baseline plus the sum of shock contributions (hd()).

ir <- irf(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "none")
round(ir$estimate[, "rate", c(1, 2, 5, 9, 17)], 3)   # responses to the policy-rate shock (Cholesky)
#>         h
#> response     0      1      4      8     16
#>    infl  0.000 -0.041 -0.058 -0.078 -0.087
#>    unemp 0.000 -0.015  0.041  0.073  0.032
#>    rate  0.715  0.555  0.385  0.219  0.077
head(tidy(ir, bands = FALSE), 3)                      # the same estimates as a tibble
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   response shock horizon estimate
#>   <fct>    <fct>   <int>    <dbl>
#> 1 infl     infl        0   0.308 
#> 2 unemp    infl        0  -0.0117
#> 3 rate     infl        0   0.0877
fv <- fevd(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "none")
round(fv$estimate[, , 17], 2)                         # rows: variable; columns: shock; horizon 16
#>         shock
#> response infl unemp rate
#>    infl  0.82  0.16 0.02
#>    unemp 0.27  0.69 0.03
#>    rate  0.40  0.26 0.34
rowSums(fv$estimate[, , 17])
#>  infl unemp  rate 
#>     1     1     1
# the impact matrix is the Cholesky factor of Sigma
round(ir$estimate[, , 1] - t(chol(fit$Sigma)), 10)
#>         shock
#> response infl unemp rate
#>    infl     0     0    0
#>    unemp    0     0    0
#>    rate     0     0    0
autoplot(fv) + labs(y = "Share of forecast error variance")

h <- hd(fit)
dim(h$contributions)                     # [time, variable, shock]
#> [1] 213   3   3
# the identity y = baseline + sum of contributions holds exactly
max(abs(h$actual - h$baseline - apply(h$contributions, c(1, 2), sum)))
#> [1] 8.881784e-16
# stacked shock contributions to inflation, actual series as the black line
autoplot(h, responses = infl)

Economic intuition / how to use it

  • IRF: the dynamic causal effect of a one-time shock, e.g. the path of unemployment after a surprise tightening. Everything depends on PP.
  • FEVD: how much of the unpredictable movement in a variable at horizon hh is attributable to each shock. A shock that explains 30% of inflation variance at horizon 16 is important for medium-run inflation fluctuations; it says nothing about the level of inflation. Because the FEVD is a ratio of squared IRFs, uncertainty about it is large and its bands are only reliable with bootstrap or Bayesian draws. At horizon 0 the FEVD is determined entirely by the ordering (the first variable’s impact variance is 100% its own shock).
  • HD: a narrative device: which shocks pushed inflation above or below its baseline in a given episode (for example, the contribution of the “rate” shock in the early 1980s). It inherits all identification assumptions, and with a single draw of a set-identified model it is conditional on that draw.

7. Normalisation, cumulative responses and ordering

Unit versus one-standard-deviation shocks. By default each column of PP gives the response to a shock of one standard deviation of the structural shock, so IRF sizes in different columns are not comparable in the units of the shock. To report “a 1 percentage-point rise in the policy rate”, rescale shock jj by 1/Θ0,ij1/\Theta_{0,ij} so the impact response of a chosen variable ii equals size: IRF̃⋅j(h)=sizeei′Θ0ejΘhej, \widetilde{\mathrm{IRF}}_{\cdot j}(h)=\frac{\mathrm{size}}{e_i'\Theta_0e_j}\,\Theta_h e_j , which is normalise = normalise_to(shock, variable, size) (the older list(shock =, variable =, size =) form still works). The normalisation applies draw by draw, so the bands are for the normalised response.

Cumulative IRFs. If a variable enters in differences, Δxt\Delta x_t, the response of its level is ∑s=0hIRFΔx(s)\sum_{s=0}^{h}\mathrm{IRF}_{\Delta x}(s). cumulative = (tidyselect) sums the responses of the selected variables over the horizon, again draw by draw (apply it before computing bands, never to the band endpoints).

ir_sd   <- irf(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "none")
ir_unit <- irf(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "none",
               normalise = normalise_to(rate, rate, 1))
round(rbind(`1 sd` = ir_sd$estimate[, "rate", 1], unit = ir_unit$estimate[, "rate", 1]), 3)
#>      infl unemp  rate
#> 1 sd    0     0 0.715
#> unit    0     0 1.000
sd_rate_shock <- ir_sd$estimate["rate", "rate", 1]
all.equal(ir_unit$estimate[, "rate", ], ir_sd$estimate[, "rate", ] / sd_rate_shock)
#> [1] TRUE
dy <- data.frame(dinfl = diff(y$infl), unemp = y$unemp[-1], rate = y$rate[-1])
fd <- varm(dy, p = 2)
ic <- irf(fd, horizon = 20, ci = "bootstrap", nboot = 300, cumulative = dinfl,
          normalise = normalise_to(rate, rate, 1))
# response of the LEVEL of inflation to a 1pp rate shock
autoplot(ic, shocks = rate, responses = dinfl) +
  labs(y = "Cumulated response of dinfl")

Ordering. With a Cholesky identification, reordering the variables changes the impact matrix and therefore every structural IRF, although the reduced-form Φh\Phi_h and the fit are unchanged. A quick robustness check is to compare orderings:

i1 <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(), horizon = 16, ci = "none")
i2 <- irf(fit, id = id_chol(order = c(rate, unemp, infl)), horizon = 16, ci = "none")
# response of unemployment to the rate shock at h = 0, 4, 8: rate ordered last versus first
round(rbind(`rate last` = i1$estimate["unemp", "rate", c(1, 5, 9)],
            `rate first` = i2$estimate["unemp", "rate", c(1, 5, 9)]), 3)
#>                 0      4     8
#> rate last   0.000  0.041 0.073
#> rate first -0.117 -0.069 0.071
round(cor(resid(fit)), 2)[3, ]
#>  infl unemp  rate 
#>  0.11 -0.35  1.00

Economic intuition / how to use it

Normalise to a meaningful unit (1pp, 25bp) whenever you compare to other studies or across methods (the LP vignette uses exactly this normalisation). Cumulate only variables that are in differences; for a level variable the plain IRF is already the level response. Ordering matters most when the residual correlations are large: the rate-with-inflation and rate-with-unemployment correlations printed above tell you how much the “rate last” assumption (the policy rate reacts to current inflation and unemployment, but they react to the rate only with a lag) matters.

8. Inference: bootstrap and Monte Carlo

All bands in varm come from the same device: a varm_draws object containing NN reduced-form pairs (B(n),Σ(n))(B^{(n)},\Sigma^{(n)}), mapped through the identification scheme one at a time. The draws() generic produces them (irf(), fevd() and forecast() call it internally when you pass ci =):

method construction when
"bootstrap" recursive design: resample residuals ût\hat u_t i.i.d., rebuild yt*y^*_t from B̂\hat B and the initial values, re-estimate homoskedastic errors, default
"wild" ut*=ηtûtu^*_t=\eta_t\hat u_t, ηt=±1\eta_t=\pm1 with probability 1/2 (Rademacher) conditional heteroskedasticity (the Great Moderation!)
"wild_mammen" ηt\eta_t from Mammen’s two-point distribution (mean 0, variance 1, skewness) skewed residuals
"mc" asymptotic draw Σ(n)∼IW(Û′Û,Te−m)\Sigma^{(n)}\sim IW(\hat U'\hat U,\,T_e-m) and vecB(n)∣Σ(n)∼N(vecB̂,Σ(n)⊗(X′X)−1)\mathrm{vec}B^{(n)}\mid\Sigma^{(n)}\sim N(\mathrm{vec}\hat B,\Sigma^{(n)}\otimes(X'X)^{-1}) fast; approximates a flat-prior Bayesian posterior

In the bootstrap variants the residuals are first centred and rescaled by Te/(Te−m)\sqrt{T_e/(T_e-m)}, and each replication re-estimates B*B^* and Σ*=Û*′Û*/(Te−m)\Sigma^*=\hat U^{*\prime}\hat U^*/(T_e-m). Draws use R’s RNG, so set.seed() makes them reproducible.

Algorithm 1: recursive-design residual (wild) bootstrap.

  1. Estimate B̂\hat B and residuals ût\hat u_t; centre and rescale them to ũt\tilde u_t.
  2. For n=1,…,Nn=1,\dots,N: set y1..p*=y1..py^*_{1..p}=y_{1..p}. Draw et*e^*_t: for the iid bootstrap et*=ũτ(t)e^*_t=\tilde u_{\tau(t)} with τ(t)\tau(t) uniform on {1,…,Te}\{1,\dots,T_e\}; for the wild bootstrap et*=ηtũte^*_t=\eta_t\tilde u_t.
  3. Build yt*=ĉ+∑lÂlyt−l*+Γ̂wt+et*y^*_t=\hat c+\sum_l\hat A_ly^*_{t-l}+\hat\Gamma w_t+e^*_t for t=p+1,…,Tt=p+1,\dots,T.
  4. Re-estimate the VAR on y*y^* to get (B(n),Σ(n))(B^{(n)},\Sigma^{(n)}).
  5. Map each draw through P(⋅)P(\cdot) to IRF/FEVD/forecast; take percentiles over nn.

The wild bootstrap keeps each residual vector ũt\tilde u_t intact in its original period (so contemporaneous correlation and time-varying variance are preserved) and multiplies it by an independent mean-zero, unit-variance scalar.

Algorithm 2: Kilian (1998) bootstrap-after-bootstrap bias correction.

  1. Run Algorithm 1 around B̂\hat B and compute b̂=B*¯−B̂\hat b=\overline{B^{*}}-\hat B.
  2. Set Bc=B̂−b̂B^c=\hat B-\hat b. If BcB^c is not stable, replace it by B̂−δb̂\hat B-\delta\hat b with the largest δ∈{1,0.99,…,0}\delta\in\{1,0.99,\dots,0\} for which the companion eigenvalues are all inside the unit circle.
  3. Recompute residuals at BcB^c and rerun Algorithm 1 around BcB^c.
  4. Correct each resulting coefficient draw in the same way, B(n)−b̂B^{(n)}-\hat b (with the same stability shrinkage), and map through P(⋅)P(\cdot). The bootstrap Σ(n)\Sigma^{(n)} draws are left as they are.

OLS is biased towards zero for persistent processes, E[Â]≈A−bE[\hat A]\approx A-b with b=O(1/T)b=O(1/T); the correction removes this to first order. With irf(bias_correct = TRUE) the bands come from the corrected draws while the point estimate returned in $estimate remains the plain sample IRF.

Two limits to keep in mind. First, bias_correct applies to bootstrap draws only ("bootstrap", "wild", "wild_mammen"): the Monte Carlo draws have no resampling step to estimate b̂\hat b from, so with method = "mc" (or ci = "mc" in irf()) the argument is ignored and a warning says so. Second, Kilian’s correction adjusts the coefficient matrix BB only; it does not bias-correct the bootstrap Σ(n)\Sigma^{(n)} draws, which are those of the bootstrap around BcB^c.

Bands are equal-tailed percentiles of the draws at each level (default 68% and 90%): $bands[response, shock, h, ] holds the quantiles at (5%,16%,84%,95%)(5\%, 16\%, 84\%, 95\%).

ir_boot <- irf(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "bootstrap", nboot = 300)
dimnames(ir_boot$bands)[[4]]
#> [1] "0.05" "0.16" "0.84" "0.95"
autoplot(ir_boot, shocks = rate)

The same bands are available in tidy form, one row per cell and level (level, conf.low, conf.high), which makes comparisons across methods a matter of subsetting a tibble:

methods <- c("bootstrap", "wild", "mc")
w90 <- sapply(methods, function(m) {
  r <- tidy(irf(fit, horizon = 16, ci = m, nboot = 300))
  r <- r[r$response == "infl" & r$shock == "rate" & r$level == 0.9 &
           r$horizon %in% c(4, 8, 16), ]
  r$conf.high - r$conf.low                                # width of the 90% band
})
rownames(w90) <- paste0("h=", c(4, 8, 16))
round(w90, 3)
#>      bootstrap  wild    mc
#> h=4      0.179 0.247 0.166
#> h=8      0.286 0.337 0.295
#> h=16     0.309 0.350 0.370
irbc <- irf(fit, horizon = 16, ci = "bootstrap", nboot = 300, bias_correct = TRUE)
band16 <- function(r) {
  r <- tidy(r)
  r <- r[r$response == "rate" & r$shock == "rate" & r$level == 0.9 & r$horizon == 16, ]
  c(conf.low = r$conf.low, conf.high = r$conf.high)
}
round(rbind(plain = band16(ir_boot), kilian = band16(irbc)), 3)
#>        conf.low conf.high
#> plain    -0.081     0.192
#> kilian   -0.120     0.357
# bias correction needs bootstrap draws: with "mc" it warns and is ignored
tryCatch(draws(fit, "mc", n = 10, bias_correct = TRUE), warning = function(w) conditionMessage(w))
#> [1] "`bias_correct` only applies to bootstrap draws; ignored for `method = \"mc\"`"

Economic intuition / how to use it

Differences between bootstrap, wild and mc bands are themselves a diagnostic: if they disagree materially, the i.i.d. Gaussian assumption is doing work and wild is the safe choice (the ARCH-LM test above is the formal version of this check). Bias correction matters when the largest eigenvalue is close to one and the horizon is long, where the uncorrected VAR understates persistence and so implies IRFs that die out too fast. The asymptotic (“mc”) bands treat B̂\hat B as exactly normal and can be too narrow at long horizons for the same reason; this is the main motivation for either bootstrap-after-bootstrap or a Bayesian VAR with a unit-root prior. Use nboot = 1000 or more for published bands; the 300 draws here are for speed.

Bands are pointwise: the 90% band at each horizon covers the true response with probability 90% for that horizon alone, so the chance that the whole path leaves the band somewhere is much larger. Simultaneous (sup-t) bands are available for local projections (lp_supt()), but not yet for VAR IRFs.

9. Forecasting

The point forecast iterates the estimated VAR forward; ŷT+h|T=ĉ+∑lÂlŷT+h−l|T\hat y_{T+h|T}=\hat c+\sum_l \hat A_l \hat y_{T+h-l|T}. With ci = "mc" (the default), "bootstrap" or "wild", the bands are predictive: each draw of (B(n),Σ(n))(B^{(n)},\Sigma^{(n)}) is combined with simulated innovations uT+s∼N(0,Σ(n))u_{T+s}\sim N(0,\Sigma^{(n)}), so they include both parameter and future-shock uncertainty. The draws themselves are in fc$draws (an unnamed array with layout [draw, horizon, variable]), from which you can compute any density summary.

fc <- forecast(fit, h = 12, ci = "mc", nboot = 500)
dimnames(fc$bands)[[3]]
#> [1] "0.05" "0.16" "0.84" "0.95"
autoplot(fc, n_history = 20)
#> Warning in ggplot2::geom_ribbon(data = d, mapping, fill = fill, alpha = 0.22, :
#> Ignoring empty aesthetic: `fill`.

head(tidy(fc), 3)               # horizon, variable, estimate, level, conf.low, conf.high
#> # A tibble: 3 × 6
#>   horizon variable estimate level conf.low conf.high
#>     <int> <fct>       <dbl> <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#> 1       1 infl         2.72   0.9     2.21      3.21
#> 2       2 infl         2.66   0.9     1.76      3.60
#> 3       3 infl         2.64   0.9     1.39      4.04

Density and fan chart. The stored draws give the full predictive distribution. A “fan” is just a set of nested quantile bands; a probability statement is an empirical frequency over draws:

dim(fc$draws)
#> [1] 500  12   3
f_rate <- fc$draws[, , 3]                           # [draw, horizon, variable]; variable 3 = rate
fan <- as.data.frame(t(apply(f_rate, 2, quantile, probs = c(0.05, 0.16, 0.5, 0.84, 0.95))))
names(fan) <- c("q05", "q16", "q50", "q84", "q95")
fan$horizon <- 1:12
ggplot(fan, aes(horizon)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q05, ymax = q95), fill = varm_palette(1), alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q16, ymax = q84), fill = varm_palette(1), alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_line(aes(y = q50), colour = varm_palette(1), linewidth = 0.9) +
  labs(x = "Quarters ahead", y = NULL, title = "Policy rate: predictive fan") +
  theme_varm()

mean(f_rate[, 12] > mean(y$rate))                    # P(rate in 12 quarters above its sample mean)
#> [1] 0.382

Economic intuition / how to use it

The fan widens and the mean reverts to the unconditional mean at the speed of the companion eigenvalues. A forecast that quickly returns to the sample mean says the model sees little persistence; if you believe the series has a unit root (random-walk interest rate, say), prefer a prior that encodes it. The bands are predictive (they include shock uncertainty), so they are far wider than the bands on the IRF. Evaluate forecasts out of sample (Section 11) rather than by in-sample fit.

10. Deterministic terms and exogenous regressors

const = TRUE (default) adds an intercept, trend = TRUE a linear trend t=1,…,Tt=1,\dots,T, and exog a T×qT\times q matrix of contemporaneous exogenous regressors wtw_t. They enter after the lags in fit$B (rows const, trend, column names of exog) and are counted in mm (and hence in the degrees of freedom and information criteria). They are not part of the companion matrix, so stability, IRFs and FEVDs refer to the endogenous dynamics only. For forecasting the future values must be known: the trend is extended automatically, exog requires exog_future (h×qh\times q).

fit_tr <- varm(y, p = 2, trend = TRUE)
round(fit_tr$B[c("const", "trend"), ], 4)
#>          infl   unemp   rate
#> const  0.2989  0.3722 0.0022
#> trend -0.0002 -0.0001 0.0001
post84 <- cbind(post84 = as.numeric(y$date >= as.Date("1984-01-01")))          # Great-Moderation dummy
fit_x <- varm(y, p = 2, exog = post84)
round(tail(fit_x$B, 3), 3)
#>           infl unemp   rate
#> rate.l2  0.061 0.045  0.124
#> const    0.302 0.364  0.010
#> post84  -0.057 0.007 -0.018
fcx <- forecast(fit_x, h = 4, exog_future = matrix(1, 4, 1), ci = "none")
round(fcx$mean, 2)
#>      infl unemp rate
#> [1,] 2.68  4.93 4.61
#> [2,] 2.57  5.06 4.41
#> [3,] 2.50  5.17 4.25
#> [4,] 2.45  5.25 4.13
c(max_eig_const = max(stability(fit)), max_eig_trend = max(stability(fit_tr)))
#> max_eig_const max_eig_trend 
#>     0.9460450     0.9446784

Economic intuition / how to use it

A trend absorbs deterministic drift and is appropriate for trending levels (log GDP); it is not a substitute for differencing a stochastic trend, and a linear trend extrapolated over a long forecast horizon is rarely credible. Exogenous regressors are for variables that are not influenced by the system: dummies for known breaks (a post-1984 dummy shifts the intercepts), oil prices for a small open economy, or a pandemic indicator. They do not produce structural shocks and their effect is excluded from the IRF; remember that forecasts condition on your assumed path for them.

11. Mistakes to avoid

Spurious regressions in levels. Regressing one random walk on another gives large R2R^2 and “significant” t-statistics with probability close to one; the t-tests of Section 2 are invalid when the regressors are integrated. A VAR in levels is still consistent (and is the right model if series may be cointegrated) but its individual t-tests are not tt-distributed; use the bootstrap bands, Wald tests only with care (Sims, Stock and Watson, 1990), and look at the largest eigenvalue.

set.seed(11)
sim <- replicate(500, {
  r <- apply(matrix(rnorm(400), 200, 2), 2, cumsum)       # two independent random walks, T = 200
  c(R2 = summary(lm(r[, 1] ~ r[, 2]))$r.squared, t = summary(lm(r[, 1] ~ r[, 2]))$coefficients[2, 3])
})
c(median_R2 = median(sim["R2", ]), rejection_rate_5pct_test = mean(abs(sim["t", ]) > 1.96))
#>                median_R2 rejection_rate_5pct_test 
#>                 0.194372                 0.846000

Too many lags. The parameter count pK2pK^2 eats degrees of freedom, makes the companion matrix noisy (spurious oscillating IRFs) and worsens out-of-sample forecasts. A pseudo out-of-sample check (expanding window, 1- and 4-step-ahead RMSE for the rate):

oos <- function(p, h, start = 120) {
  e <- sapply(start:(nrow(y) - h), function(t) {
    f <- varm(y[1:t, ], p = p)
    forecast(f, h = h, ci = "none")$mean[h, "rate"] - y$rate[t + h]
  })
  sqrt(mean(e^2))
}
res <- sapply(c(1, 2, 4, 8), function(p) c(h1 = oos(p, 1), h4 = oos(p, 4)))
colnames(res) <- paste0("p=", c(1, 2, 4, 8))
round(res, 3)
#>     p=1   p=2   p=4   p=8
#> h1 0.55 0.499 0.528 0.558
#> h4 1.51 1.275 1.305 1.393

Ordering without thought. A Cholesky ordering is an economic assumption, not a technicality (Section 7). Reading individual coefficients as causal effects, reading pointwise bands as simultaneous, ignoring residual diagnostics (Section 5), and using mc bands with persistent data (Section 8) are the other common errors. Finally, a bootstrap that includes an unstable draw has an explosive IRF; check stability(draws(fit, "bootstrap", 300)) for the share of non-stationary replications:

mean(apply(stability(draws(fit, "bootstrap", 500)), 1, max) >= 1)
#> [1] 0

12. Speed

The estimation loop, the bootstrap and the IRF mapping are all compiled (RcppArmadillo). On an Apple M4 Pro a varm() fit takes about 0.05 ms, a 1000-draw wild bootstrap about 0.02 s, and an impulse response with bands from 1000 wild draws about 0.03 s. The chunk below re-measures these on your machine (timings vary with hardware and load):

t_fit <- system.time(for (i in 1:100) varm(y, p = 2))[["elapsed"]] / 100
t_draw <- system.time(draws(fit, "wild", n = 1000))[["elapsed"]]
t_irf <- system.time(irf(fit, horizon = 20, ci = "wild", nboot = 1000))[["elapsed"]]
c(varm_ms = 1000 * t_fit, wild_1000_draws_sec = t_draw, irf_1000_wild_draws_sec = t_irf)
#>                 varm_ms     wild_1000_draws_sec irf_1000_wild_draws_sec 
#>                   0.250                   0.043                   0.059

Extensions

Pending: simultaneous (sup-t) bands for VAR impulse responses; the local-projection analogue is already available as lp_supt() (vignette("local-projections")).
